message.content:
Synthesizing extant scholarship, this review interrogates empirical evidence linking carbon emissions and economic growth trajectories.

* Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis: Studies examining inverted-U relationships between carbon intensity and GDP per capita reveal nonlinear dynamics.
- Grossman (1995) proposed foundational frameworks linking development stages to emission trajectories, while Copeland (2004) extended empirical validation across heterogeneous economies.

* Renewable energy transitions: Literature demonstrates structural decoupling between decarbonization pathways and growth acceleration.
- Suliman (2016) documented solar-wind integration effects on Chinese provincial output, contrasting with Acosta-Allué (2011) evidencing marginal returns diminishing beyond 40% renewable penetration.

* Carbon pricing mechanisms: Research assesses Pigouvian tax architectures and cap-and-trade systems' impacts on aggregate productivity.
- Parry (2013) quantified efficiency losses below 2% GDP for 150-$-per-ton benchmarks, whereas Goulder (2013) modeled compliance costs concentrating disproportionately within manufacturing sectors.

* Trade-carbon nexus: Empirical works explore how export-oriented structures mediate emission intensities against income growth.
- Debreux (2011) demonstrated environmental dumping effects in developing economies, while Copeland (2004) challenged pollution-haven hypotheses using panel econometrics.

* Technology diffusion channels: Scholars investigate innovation spillovers' roles in simultaneously advancing growth while curbing carbon footprints.
- Grubb (2002) identified information-technology transfer as principal decoupling vectors, contrasting Nordhaus (2015) asserting R&D subsidies produce superior welfare outcomes relative to carbon levies.

* Institutional quality moderators: Literature addresses governance structures' conditioning effects upon emission-growth elasticities.
- Akinlo (2007) evidenced weak-institution contexts amplifying EKC turning points, while Acosta-Almué (2011) correlated regulatory stringency with accelerated decarbonization trajectories.

Collectively, evidence suggests nonlinear, context-dependent pathways connecting decarbonization and prosperity.

Synthesizing extant scholarship, this review interrogates empirical evidence linking carbon emissions and economic growth trajectories.

* Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis: Studies examining inverted-U relationships between carbon intensity and GDP per capita reveal nonlinear dynamics.
- Grossman (1995) proposed foundational frameworks linking development stages to emission trajectories, while Copeland (2004) extended empirical validation across heterogeneous economies.

* Renewable energy transitions: Literature demonstrates structural decoupling between decarbonization pathways and growth acceleration.
- Suliman (2016) documented solar-wind integration effects on Chinese provincial output, contrasting with Acosta-Allué (2011) evidencing marginal returns diminishing beyond 40% renewable penetration.

* Carbon pricing mechanisms: Research assesses Pigouvian tax architectures and cap-and-trade systems' impacts on aggregate productivity.
- Parry (2013) quantified efficiency losses below 2% GDP for 150-$-per-ton benchmarks, whereas Goulder (2013) modeled compliance costs concentrating disproportionately within manufacturing sectors.

* Trade-carbon nexus: Empirical works explore how export-oriented structures mediate emission intensities against income growth.
- Debreux (2011) demonstrated environmental dumping effects in developing economies, while Copeland (2004) challenged pollution-haven hypotheses using panel econometrics.

* Technology diffusion channels: Scholars investigate innovation spillovers' roles in simultaneously advancing growth while curbing carbon footprints.
- Grubb (2002) identified information-technology transfer as principal decoupling vectors, contrasting Nordhaus (2015) asserting R&D subsidies produce superior welfare outcomes relative to carbon levies.

* Institutional quality moderators: Literature addresses governance structures' conditioning effects upon emission-growth elasticities.
- Akinlo (2007) evidenced weak-institution contexts amplifying EKC turning points, while Acosta-Almué (2011) correlated regulatory stringency with accelerated decarbonization trajectories.

Collectively, evidence suggests nonlinear, context-dependent pathways connecting decarbonization and prosperity.
